content: Pantothenic acid, also known as vitamin B5, is a water-soluble vitamin that is essential for sustaining life. It plays a critical role in the formation of coenzyme A (CoA), which is necessary for the metabolism and synthesis of carbohydrates, proteins, and fats. Chemically, pantothenic acid is an amide formed between D-pantoate and beta-alanine. Its name is derived from the Greek word pantothen, meaning from everywhere, as small amounts of pantothenic acid are found in nearly all foods. Foods particularly rich in pantothenic acid include whole grain cereals, legumes, eggs, meat, and royal jelly. It is often found in its alcohol analog form, panthenol, or as calcium pantothenate. Only the dextrorotatory (D) isomer of pantothenic acid is biologically active, while the levorotatory (L) form may counteract the effects of the active isomer. Pantothenic acid is essential for the synthesis of coenzyme A, which functions as a carrier of acyl groups to form acetyl-CoA and other related compounds. This process is vital for the transport of carbon atoms within cells. Coenzyme A is involved in cellular respiration and the biosynthesis of critical compounds such as fatty acids, cholesterol, and acetylcholine. Because of its involvement in numerous essential biological processes, pantothenic acid is indispensable for all forms of life. Deficiencies in this vitamin can lead to a wide range of effects. Pantothenic acid is present in small amounts in most foods, with higher concentrations in whole grains and eggs. It is also available in dietary supplements, often in the form of calcium-D-pantothenate. Some beverages are now fortified with pantothenic acid. Additionally, research suggests that gut bacteria in humans may produce pantothenic acid. The active form of pantothenic acid in the body is pantethine, but it is unstable at high temperatures or during prolonged storage. Therefore, calcium pantothenate is the more commonly used form in dietary supplements. Ten milligrams of calcium pantothenate is equivalent to 9.2 milligrams of pantothenic acid. In the United Kingdom, the recommended daily allowance (RDA) is 6 milligrams per day. Deficiency of pantothenic acid is extremely rare and has not been extensively studied. In the few documented cases, such as in individuals experiencing starvation or in controlled volunteer trials, symptoms were reversible upon reintroduction of the vitamin. Symptoms of deficiency are generally mild and include fatigue, allergies, nausea, and abdominal pain. In rare cases, more severe but reversible conditions, such as adrenal insufficiency and hepatic encephalopathy, have been observed. A notable symptom reported in volunteer trials was a painful burning sensation in the feet, which may explain similar complaints from malnourished prisoners of war. Despite the rarity of deficiency, pantothenic acid has been explored for various alternative uses. In the field of hair care, severe pantothenic acid deficiency in mouse models was associated with skin irritation and loss of hair color. This led the cosmetic industry to incorporate pantothenic acid into products like shampoos. However, human trials have not demonstrated any benefits, yet many cosmetic products continue to advertise pantothenic acid as an additive. In the late 1990s, a small study by Dr. Lit-Hung Leung suggested that high doses of pantothenic acid could treat acne vulgaris. The study proposed that coenzyme A regulates hormones and fatty acids, and insufficient pantothenic acid may lead to an imbalance, causing fatty acids to accumulate and be excreted through sebaceous glands, resulting in acne. Dr. Leung administered 10-20 grams of pantothenic acid daily (100,000%-200,000% of the US Daily Value) to 45 Asian males and 55 Asian females, with 80% taken orally and 20% applied topically. Improvement in acne was reported within one week to one month. However, the study has been criticized for its lack of a double-blind, placebo-controlled design, and no further studies have confirmed these findings. Additionally, there is no evidence supporting the claim that acetyl-CoA prioritizes androgen regulation over fatty acid metabolism during stress or limited availability. Pantothenic acid has also been studied in combination with alpha-lipoic acid for the treatment of diabetic peripheral polyneuropathy. In one study, 28 out of 33 patients (84.8%) who had previously been treated with alpha-lipoic acid reported further improvement when pantothenic acid was added. The proposed mechanism is that both substances act on different aspects of pyruvate metabolism, making the combination more effective than either substance alone. Clinical findings also suggest that diabetic neuropathy may be associated with latent prediabetic metabolic disturbances and that symptoms can be favorably influenced by this combination therapy, even in cases of poorly controlled diabetes. Today, many companies market vitamin B5 supplements for acne treatment. However, the recommended treatment regimen can be challenging and expensive. Some protocols suggest starting with 5 grams per day for the first three days, then increasing to 10 grams daily for three months. Since the largest available pill is typically 1 gram, this could require taking up to 10 pills per day or more if smaller doses are used. A bottle of 200 tablets containing 500 milligrams each costs approximately $10, making the treatment costly. Alternatively, pantothenic acid is available as a powder that can be dissolved in water, which may be a more affordable and convenient option for some individuals. After three months, many users reduce their intake to 3-5 grams per day, with some finding 1 gram per day sufficient. Pantothenic acid is also known by other names, including pantothenate, vitamin B5, and Vilantae (a brand name used for acne treatment).
